terms.grammar: pronoun, first person: dative mihi, accusative and ablative mē; plural nōs
evidence: Cic. Att. 5.1.3: tū invītā mulierēs, ego virōs accīverō
terms.comment: Latin leaves the subject out: the ending of the verb already says “I” (intellegō). Ego is said only for stress or contrast, as in “you invite the women, I’ll fetch the men”; a needless ego at every turn is English underneath. “It’s me” is Ego sum. “With me” is mēcum, the preposition put after the pronoun.

terms.gloss: I myself, I for my part
evidence: Plaut. Am. 2.1.60: Quis tē verberāvit? — Egomet mēmet. (Lewis & Short, s.v. ego)
terms.comment: A stronger ego; the suffix -met also strengthens the other cases (mēmet, mihimet, nōsmet).

phrases.english: You keep on at me, though I understand.

phrases.latin: Pompōnia, inquit, tū invītā mulierēs, ego virōs accīverō
phrases.english: “Pomponia,” he said, “you invite the women, and I’ll have fetched the men.”

phrases.latin: sī valēs, bene est; ego valeō
phrases.english: If you are well, good; I am well.

phrases.latin: Num tū intellegis hīc quid narret? — Num tū? — Nihil. — Tantundem ego.
phrases.english: Do you understand what he’s saying? — Do you? — Not a thing. — No more do I.

phrases.latin: heus, ecquis hīc est? ecquis hoc aperit ōstium? — Quis ad forēs est? — Ego sum.
phrases.english: Hey, is anyone there? Will anyone open this door? — Who’s at the door? — It’s me.

phrases.latin: salvē, inquit illa; cūr mē fūgistī, obsecrō?
phrases.english: “Hello,” she said; “why did you run away from me, please?”
For a long time now you’ve sent me no letters.
